Decision problems in urban transportation systems can have huge socio-economic impact, which need careful analysis in various levels of resolution and an efficient optimization framework.

general, these systems are complex (e.g., dynamic, stochastic, non-linear) and difficult to model analytically, which precludes the use of traditional optimization methods. A powerful alternative is simulation-enabled approach. Recently, a variety of commercial or open-source traffic simulation tools have been developed, providing us

comprehensive way to capture the intricate interactions between the demand and the supply components of the mobility networks. In current practices, there are widely applied traffic simulators such as microscopic ones (e.g., VISSIM, PARAMICS, SUMO) and macroscopic ones (e.g., VISUM, DTALITE, DYNUST). The former focuses on simulating traffic flow dynamics by detailed modeling of driver behavior, while the latter focuses on flow distributions on larger networks with only aggregate traffic flow model on each link. These microscopic and macroscopic traffic simulators can provide estimates of traffic network performance under various system uncertainties (e.g., random traffic
volume inputs, random driving and routing behaviors, et
.). These tools are therefore often used to evaluate and compare a set of predetermined solutions (e.g., traffic facility locations or network design plans)
in the context of what-if analysis or sensitivity analysis for better decision-making.

As noted earlier, the BO approach has two fundamental components: the belief model describing subjective probability distribution over the solutions as well as the sampling policy based on the acquisition function defined for the solutions. While the GP is the most-commonly adopted belief model in BO, the options for sampling policies are more diversified. In particular, many studies adopt the KG
policy for the sampling decisions in BO

whose main advantages are mentioned in Section 1. The KG policy chooses the next solution (or alternative) to be sampled which has the largest KG-factor, i.e., the expected improvement in the best posterior mean conditional on all
previous samples. Such a methodology was shown to be effective and empirically
efficient for many SO applications compared to many other approaches. The KG policy was firstly introduced in Gupta and Miescke (1996) for the independent belief case
where the unknown mean of the performance of each solution has an independent prior distribution. Frazier (200
proved serval key properties of the KG policy such as asymptotic optimality and
derived a more general KG policy for correlated beliefs, where the prior mean vector follows a multi-variate Gaussian distribution

which was shown to outperform other batch BO algorithms.

3 Network-wide Signal Timing Problem under Uncertainties (NSTPU)

Urban signalized intersections are not only the bottleneck of traffic efficiency and dense area of vehicular emissions, but also influence the equity of right-of-way in the urban road network. In this condition, traffic efficiency is set as an evaluation indicator rather than the only indicator, when designing the traffic control system. Specifically, the traffic equity has been considered in various traffic control problems, such as temporal and spatial inequities of ramp metering control (Levinson and Zhang 2006), aggregated and non-aggregated equity indices of corridor control (Ma and Zhang 2008), spatial equity index of dynamic ramp control (Meng and Khoo 2010), travel time-based Atkinson index of network-wide traffic signal timing plan (Zheng et al. 2019a). Meanwhile, traffic signal control plan substantially affects the driving modes of vehicles which would result in various intensities of vehicular emissions.

specifically, vehicular emissions tend to decrease when the vehicle is accelerating, cruising, decelerating and idling (Unal et al. 2003), and increase considerably if vehicle stops are introduced (Rakha and Ding 2003). Thus, apart from traffic efficiency, vehicular emissions on signalized traffic networks are greatly influenced by the traffic signal control plan. SO approach for bi-objective stochastic optimization problems with probabilistic constraints and applied it to a nontrivial traffic network control problem which involves a very large number of feasible solutions. The challenges of these type of problems lie in effective learning of both the mean values of the two objectives as well as the quantile of the constraint function, particularly when the decision space is large. Therefore, we designed a flexible parametric GPR based posterior distribution over the feasible solutions and proposed an efficient approximate knowledge gradient sampling policy.
